title: Disinformation among students arriving at university to pursue degrees related with information science. The cases of Brazil, Cuba and Spain (La desinformación en los alumnos que llegan a la universidad en las titulaciones relacionadas con la Information Science)
screen_reason: Cross-sectional 26-item survey of 428 first-year information-science students at 16 public universities in Brazil, Cuba and Spain (answers collected September 2022 - July 2023). Most items measure competence/knowledge (defining infodemic, clickbait, bots, spotting a satire item) or hypothetical reactions, which are not eligible. One item is an eligible self-reported behavioural share: question 16, '¿Alguna vez has compartido algún tipo de información, sabiendo que podría ser desinformación, sin verificar antes la fuente?' ('Have you ever shared any kind of information, knowing it might be disinformation, without first verifying the source?'), reported as Yes/No shares of respondents by country (Brazil 27 %, Spain 36.5 %, Cuba 25.9 %) and pooled in the abstract and conclusion (31.5 %). That is a share of survey respondents who say they shared misinformation, i.e. RECALL with recall_subtype sharing.

estimates.misinfo_def: La desinformación (disinformation) es definida como "la difusión intencionada de información no rigurosa que busca minar la confianza pública, distorsionar los hechos, transmitir una determinada forma de percibir la realidad y explotar vulnerabilidades con el objetivo de desestabilizar" (Olmo y Romeo, 2019). [Translation: Disinformation is defined as "the intentional dissemination of inaccurate information that seeks to undermine public trust, distort facts, transmit a particular way of perceiving reality and exploit vulnerabilities in order to destabilise".]

estimates.notes: QUOTE RENDERING: the source_quote is the verbatim, contiguous text of the Tabla 12 block as the PDF extraction renders it, which interleaves the question stem with the three country rows. Reconstructed reading: '¿Alguna vez ha compartido algún tipo de información, sabiendo que podría ser información errónea, sin verificar primero la fuente? Brasil: Sí 53 (27%) / No 143 (72,9%); España: Sí 75 (36,5%) / No 130 (63,4%); Cuba: Sí 7 (25,9%) / No 20 (74%)'. English translation: 'Have you ever shared any kind of information, knowing it might be misinformation, without first verifying the source? Brazil: yes 53 (27%), no 143 (72.9%); Spain: yes 75 (36.5%), no 130 (63.4%); Cuba: yes 7 (25.9%), no 20 (74%)'. Lifetime ('¿Alguna vez...?') self-report, no time window. Sample is first-year university students in information-science degrees, recruited through teachers of compulsory first-year courses at universities that answered the invitation, so population_scope=other (students) and sampling_frame=convenience. The pooled three-country figure (31.5 %) is stated verbatim in the abstract and conclusion but is not extracted as a separate row to avoid double counting; see missed_or_uncertain.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) POOLED VALUE AVAILABLE BUT NOT ROWED: the pooled three-country share for the same item is stated verbatim twice - abstract, 'la cantidad de encuestados (31,5%) que afirmaron haber compartido algún tipo de desinformación' ('the number of respondents (31.5 %) who reported having shared some kind of disinformation'), and conclusion, 'los encuestados que afirmaron haber compartido algún tipo de desinformación (31,5%)'. It equals 135/428. I extracted the three country rows the paper reports rather than the pooled figure to avoid double counting; if the review prefers one row per study, use 31.5 % of 428 (Multi-country: Brazil, Cuba, Spain) with the same moderator coding. (2) NOT EXTRACTED - not prevalence: Table 11 attitudes to disinformation, including the widely quoted 34.8 % who 'simplemente dejé de leer e ignoré la información' ('simply stopped reading and ignored the information'). The English abstract mistranslates this as students 'who are unaware of how much incorrect information they receive'; the Spanish makes clear it is a behavioural reaction to misinformation received, not a share exposed, so it is not an exposure estimate. Question 14 is also worded counterfactually ('recibiste (o hubieses recibido)' - 'you received (or had you received)'), mixing actual and hypothetical behaviour. (3) NOT EXTRACTED - competence/knowledge, not prevalence: correct identification of 'infodemia' (83.1 %), of the satire item (46.9 %), of clickbait as a false connection (14 %), of the purpose of bots (52.1 %), of fake news (97 %/94 %/85 %), and of post-truth definitions; and Table 9 verification criteria (64.2 % always verify at the original source, 36.6 % rely on prior knowledge, 5.3 % assume anything online is true). These are literacy/behaviour measures with no misinformation numerator. (4) Table 12's companion item ('would you tell the person the information is not reliable', 87.2 %/85.3 %/74 %) is a hypothetical reaction, excluded. (5) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY for an adjudicator: Table 9 reports 275 (64.2 %) for 'siempre verifico la información en su fuente original', while the abstract and conclusion give 265 (61.9 %) for the same item; likewise Table 8's 'Otros' column sums to 49 but is labelled 22.2 %. These affect items I did not extract, but they signal loose table-keeping in this paper. (6) Data-collection year coded 2022 (September 2022 - July 2023 window); publication year is 2024.

rob.design: Cross-sectional self-administered online survey (Google Forms; 26 closed and open items, Spanish and Portuguese versions) of students beginning information-science-related degrees at 16 public universities in Brazil (10), Spain (5) and Cuba (1). Recruitment was by convenience: teachers of compulsory first-year courses, known to the authors or reached through course coordinators, e-mailed the link to their students in the first two to three weeks of classes; 21 coordinators/teachers participated. 428 respondents (Brazil 196, Spain 205, Cuba 27). No sampling frame size, no response rate, and no non-response analysis are reported; no instrument validation, no test-retest, no reliability statistics; analysis was descriptive cross-tabulation in Excel. Two internal numerical inconsistencies between tables and the abstract/conclusion (64.2 % vs 61.9 % for the source-verification item).
